issues.legal_issue: A tenant may challenge whether an acquisition relied on to seek eviction was a bona fide transaction, and that challenge must be decided on the evidence rather than rejected solely because the tenant was not a party to the transaction.
material_facts: The tenant alleged that the landlord’s purchase was a sham transaction made to create a ground for eviction, and contended that the sellers had not received the sale consideration.
The appellate authority rejected the challenge because the tenant was not a party to the sale deed and did not allow the tenant to refer to evidence on the issue.
The High Court did not address whether the sale was bona fide.
issues.conclusion: The eviction decree was set aside and the case was remitted for a finding, on the evidence already available and any further evidence the court considered necessary, on whether the sale was bona fide.
issues.legal_principle: A tenant’s lack of party status in a sale does not prevent the tenant from challenging an allegation that the sale was a sham. Where that allegation is material to the eviction claim, the court must determine it on the evidence. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on.

predicates.eviction_proceeding: The case is a proceeding in which a landlord seeks eviction of a tenant.
predicates.tenant_challenges_landlord_acquisition_a: The tenant alleges that the landlord’s acquisition was not genuine and was made to create a basis for eviction.
predicates.challenge_rejected_only_for_lack_of_part: The court declines to decide the tenant’s challenge solely because the tenant was not a party to the acquisition.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding involves a tenant’s sham-acquisition challenge that was rejected only for lack of party status, the eviction decree is set aside and the question of the acquisition’s bona fides is remitted for decision.
